snip.t: Leads to Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS): anuria, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), hepatic necrosis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

Multiorgan Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS): Prolonged tissue hypoperfusion precipitates acute kidney injury (acute tubular necrosis), ischaemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), stress ulceration, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC): Endothelial damage, release of procoagulant factors.
Concomitant septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), or extensive purpura fulminans.

qs.q: How does the coagulation profile typically present in patients with hemolytic uremic syndrome compared to disseminated intravascular coagulation?
o: Clotting is normal in HUS due to localized intravascular thrombogenesis
Both conditions exhibit severely prolonged prothrombin time values
Clotting factors are completely depleted within HUS patients
Thrombin time is markedly decreased in disseminated intravascular coagulation
qs.e: In HUS, the toxin causes localized intravascular thrombogenesis, activating the coagulation cascade while clotting remains normal. This distinguishes it from disseminated intravascular coagulation where systemic clotting abnormalities occur.

qs.q: Why does Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) occur during an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction?
o: Exogenous heparin in stored blood depletes coagulation factors
Lysed red cells release thromboplastin, triggering widespread clotting
Complement activation selectively destroys circulating platelets first
Renal vasoconstriction induces hepatic synthesis of abnormal fibrinogen
qs.e: When red cells lyse during an acute haemolytic reaction, they release thromboplastin which triggers widespread, uncontrolled clotting and consumes all clotting factors. Stored blood contains citrate rather than heparin, which does not cause consumptive coagulopathy.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion Contraindications & Acute Reactions — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which laboratory test is considered the most sensitive and specific marker for diagnosing disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
o: Bleeding Time measured in minutes
D-dimer measured in the plasma
Thrombin Time measured in seconds
Platelet Count measured in volume
qs.e: D-dimer is a fibrinolysis marker and serves as the most sensitive test for DIC. Bleeding time assesses platelet function and vessel wall interaction rather than systemic fibrin breakdown.

qs.q: A patient presents with acute febrile illness, jaundice, and spontaneous bleeding following direct exposure to aborted animal tissues in an abattoir. Laboratory findings reveal severe liver damage and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which family does the causative agent belong to?
o: Bunyaviridae family
Picornaviridae family
Flaviviridae family
Hepadnaviridae family
qs.e: Rift Valley Fever Virus belongs to the family Bunyaviridae and can cause severe manifestations like hemorrhagic fever with liver damage and jaundice. Supportive care is the mainstay as no specific antiviral is licensed.

qs.q: According to Rudolf Virchow's triad of factors leading to intravascular coagulation, which of the following represents the component associated with immobility and paralysis?
o: Stasis
Endothelial injury
Hypercoagulability
Local trauma
qs.e: Immobility, paralysis, and obesity are clinical conditions that lead to blood stasis, which is one part of Virchow's triad. Endothelial injury and hypercoagulability are the other two components.

qs.q: What is the pathophysiological hallmark of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
o: Widespread intravascular fibrin formation due to excessive protease activity
Isolated platelet deficiency without any associated fibrin deposition
Primary hyperfibrinolysis occurring without prior activation of coagulation
Autoimmune destruction targeting specific circulating clotting factors
qs.e: DIC is defined by widespread fibrin formation that overwhelms natural anticoagulants. The other options describe mechanisms not central to DIC.

qs.q: What is the primary pathophysiological definition of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?
o: Widespread intravascular fibrin formation due to excessive blood protease activity
Isolated localized thrombosis occurring within deep venous vascular systems
Primary bone marrow failure leading to absolute amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia
Autosomal recessive deficiency of coagulation factors II, VII, and X
qs.e: DIC is defined as a clinico-pathological syndrome characterized by widespread intravascular fibrin formation in response to excessive blood protease activity. It is distinct from isolated venous thrombosis or primary bone marrow failure.

qs.q: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) laboratory profile includes
o: High fibrinogen, low D-dimer, prolonged PT
Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT/APTT
Normal PT, elevated fibrinogen, high platelets
Isolated thrombocytopaenia with normal coagulation
qs.e: Systemic clotting consumes fibrinogen, factors, and platelets while fibrinolysis elevates D-dimers; both PT and APTT are prolonged.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Intravascular coagulation is a systemic activation of clotting that paradoxically causes both microthrombi and bleeding. It is a consumptive coagulopathy seen in sepsis, trauma, and malignancy.

sections.p: Intravascular coagulation refers to widespread activation of the coagulation cascade within vessels, leading to consumption of platelets and clotting factors. Diagnosis is clinical plus laboratory evidence of consumption: prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer, thrombocytopenia.

t.b: Low platelets indicate consumption; <50×10^9/L suggests severe DIC.
Prolonged times reflect factor consumption; >1.5× normal is concerning.
Low (<1.5 g/L) shows consumption; high levels may be acute phase reactant.
Elevated (>5 µg/mL) indicates fibrin degradation; very high values support DIC.

sections.p: Severity is staged by the ISTH scoring system: points for platelet count, fibrinogen, PT prolongation, D‑dimer, and fibrinogen degradation products. Scores ≥5 indicate overt DIC.
b: ISTH score 0–4: non‑overt; 5–6: overt, mild; 7–8: overt, severe

sections.p: The most common triggers are sepsis, severe trauma, obstetric complications, and malignancy. In low‑resource settings, infections such as malaria, TB, HIV, and bacterial sepsis are frequent.
b: Infections common in tropics (malaria, TB, HIV)

sections.p: Patients may have petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, or organ ischemia manifesting as organ dysfunction. Bleeding may be spontaneous or after minor trauma.
Lab tests confirm consumptive coagulopathy and help rule out other causes. Point‑of‑care tests are useful when full labs are unavailable.

t.b: Detects thrombocytopenia; severe drop suggests consumption.
Prolongation indicates factor loss; helps differentiate from inherited coagulopathies.
Low levels confirm consumption; normal or high levels may mask DIC.
High levels support fibrin formation and breakdown; very high values are typical in DIC.

sections.p: Urgent bleeding, sudden organ failure, or unexplained shock require immediate care. Complications include multi‑organ failure, limb ischemia, and death.

faq.q: Can DIC be present without obvious bleeding?
faq.a: Yes, microthrombi can cause organ ischemia before overt bleeding appears.

faq.q: Is anticoagulation ever used in DIC?
faq.a: Only when thrombosis predominates and bleeding risk is low; otherwise, it is avoided.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of DIC in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Severe bacterial sepsis, often from malaria, TB, or HIV infections.
